danish.title: Femtende bog (1812–13) — Kapitel 15
paragraphs: I slutningen af januar tog Pierre til Moskva og boede i en sidefløj af sit hus, der ikke var brændt ned. Han aflagde besøg hos grev Rostopchin og nogle bekendte, der var vendt tilbage til Moskva, og agtede at rejse til Petersborg to dage senere. Alle fejrede sejren, alt boblede af liv i den ødelagte, men genopstående by. Alle var glade for at se Pierre, alle ønskede at møde ham, og alle udspurgte ham om, hvad han havde oplevet. Pierre følte sig særligt venligt stemt over for dem alle, men var nu instinktivt på vagt for ikke at binde sig på nogen måde. Til alle spørgsmål — hvad enten de var vigtige eller helt ligegyldige — som: Hvor ville han bo? Ville han bygge op igen? Hvornår skulle han til Petersborg, og kunne han tage en pakke med? — svarede han: »Ja, måske« eller: »Det tror jeg nok« og så videre.

Han havde hørt, at familien Rostov var i Kostroma, men tanken om Natasja (Rostova) faldt ham sjældent ind. Hvis den gjorde, var det kun som et behageligt minde om den fjerne fortid. Han følte sig fri, ikke blot for sociale forpligtelser, men også for den følelse, han mente selv at have fremkaldt.

På tredje dagen efter sin ankomst hørte han fra familien Drubetskoj, at fyrstinde Marja var i Moskva. Fyrst Andrejs (Bolkonskijs) død, lidelser og sidste dage havde ofte optaget Pierres tanker og vendte nu tilbage med fornyet styrke. Da han ved middagen hørte, at fyrstinde Marja var i Moskva og boede i sit hus — der ikke var brændt — i Vozdvizjenka-gaden, kørte han samme aften derhen for at besøge hende.
På vej til huset tænkte Pierre ustandselig på fyrst Andrej, på deres venskab, deres forskellige møder og især det sidste ved Borodino.

»Mon han døde i den bitre sindstilstand, han var i dengang? Mon livets mening blev åbenbaret for ham, inden han døde?« tænkte Pierre. Han mindedes Karatajev (Platon Karatajev) og hans død og begyndte uvilkårligt at sammenligne disse to mænd, så forskellige og dog så ens i, at de begge havde levet og begge var døde, og i den kærlighed, han følte for dem begge.

Pierre kørte op foran den gamle fyrsts hus i en højst alvorlig stemning. Huset havde undgået ilden; det viste tegn på skade, men dets almene udseende var uforandret. Den gamle lakaj, der mødte Pierre med et strengt ansigt, som ville han give den besøgende at føle, at den gamle fyrstes fravær ikke havde forstyrret husets orden, meddelte, at fyrstinden var gået op til sine egne gemakker, og at hun tog imod om søndagen.
»Meld mig. Måske vil hun tage imod mig,« sagde Pierre.
»Ja, Deres Excellence,« sagde manden. »Vær så venlig at gå ind i portrætgalleriet.«

Få minutter senere vendte lakajen tilbage med Dessalles, der bragte besked fra fyrstinden om, at hun med glæde ville modtage Pierre, hvis han ville undskylde manglen på formaliteter og komme op til hendes gemakker.

I et ret lavloftet rum, oplyst af ét lys, sad fyrstinden og hos hende en anden person klædt i sort. Pierre huskede, at fyrstinden altid havde selskabsdamer, men hvem de var, og hvordan de så ud, vidste eller huskede han aldrig. »Det må være en af hendes selskabsdamer,« tænkte han og kastede et blik på damen i den sorte kjole.
Fyrstinden rejste sig hurtigt for at møde ham og rakte ham hånden.

»Ja,« sagde hun og betragtede hans forandrede ansigt, efter at han havde kysset hendes hånd, »så det er altså sådan, vi mødes igen. Han talte om Dem helt til det sidste,« fortsatte hun og vendte blikket fra Pierre til sin ledsagerske med en generthed, der et øjeblik overraskede ham.
»Jeg var så glad for at høre, at De var i sikkerhed. Det var det første gode nyt, vi havde modtaget i lang tid.«
Atter kastede fyrstinden et blik på sin ledsagerske med endnu større uro i sine manérer og var ved at tilføje noget, men Pierre afbrød hende.

»Tænk Dem — jeg vidste intet om ham!« sagde han. »Jeg troede, han var faldet. Alt, hvad jeg ved, har jeg hørt på anden hånd fra andre. Jeg ved kun, at han blev optaget af familien Rostov.... Sikke en mærkelig tilfældighed!«

Pierre talte hurtigt og livligt. Han kastede et blik på ledsagerskindens ansigt, så hendes opmærksomme og venlige blik rettet mod ham, og følte — som det ofte sker, når man taler — at denne ledsagerske i den sorte kjole var et godt, venligt, fortræffeligt menneske, der ikke ville hindre hans frie samtale med fyrstinde Marja.
Men da han nævnte familien Rostov, udtrykte fyrstinde Marjas ansigt endnu større forlegenhed. Hun kastede atter et hurtigt blik fra Pierres ansigt til den sortklædte dames ansigt og sagde:
»Genkender De hende virkelig ikke?«
Pierre så atter på ledsagerskindens blege, fine ansigt med de sorte øjne og den ejendommelige mund, og noget nært, længe glemt og mere end smukt så på ham fra de opmærksomme øjne.

»Men nej, det kan ikke være!« tænkte han. »Det strenge, tynde, blege ansigt, der ser så meget ældre ud! Det kan ikke være hende. Det minder mig blot om hende.« Men i det øjeblik sagde fyrstinde Marja: »Natasja!« Og med besvær, anstrengelse og pres, som en dør der har sat sig fast på rustne hængsler, viste et smil sig på ansigtet med de opmærksomme øjne, og fra den åbnede dør kom et pust af duft, der overstrømmede Pierre med en lykke, han længe havde glemt, og som han ikke engang havde tænkt på — især ikke i det øjeblik. Den overstrømmede ham, greb ham og indhyllede ham fuldstændig. Da hun smilede, var tvivlen ikke længere mulig — det var Natasja, og han elskede hende.

I det øjeblik forrådte Pierre uvilkårligt for hende, for fyrstinde Marja og frem for alt for sig selv en hemmelighed, han ikke selv havde været klar over. Han rødmede af glæde, men med smertelig uro. Han forsøgte at skjule sin ophidselse. Men jo mere han forsøgte at skjule den, desto tydeligere — tydeligere end nogen ord kunne have gjort — forrådte han for sig selv, for hende og for fyrstinde Marja, at han elskede hende.

»Nej, det er bare det uventede,« tænkte Pierre. Men så snart han forsøgte at genoptage den samtale, han havde begyndt med fyrstinde Marja, kastede han atter et blik på Natasja, og en endnu dybere rødme bredte sig over hans ansigt, og en endnu stærkere uro af blandet glæde og frygt greb hans sjæl. Han blev forvirret i sin tale og standsede midt i det, han sagde.

Pierre havde overset Natasja, fordi han slet ikke forventede at se hende dér, men han havde ikke genkendt hende, fordi forandringen, siden han sidst havde set hende, var enorm. Hun var blevet tynd og bleg, men det var ikke det, der gjorde hende ugenkendelig; hun var ugenkendelig i det øjeblik, han trådte ind, fordi på det ansigt, hvis øjne altid havde strålet med et undertrykt smil af livsglæde, var der nu, da han trådte ind og betragtede hende, ikke den mindste antydning af smil: kun venlige, opmærksomme og sørgeligt spørgende øjne.
Pierres forvirring afspejledes ikke i nogen forvirring fra Natasjas side, men kun i den glæde, der lige akkurat mærkbart oplyste hele hendes ansigt.

english.title: Book Fifteen (1812 - 13) — Chapter 15
paragraphs: At the end of January, Pierre arrived in Moscow and stayed in a wing of his house that hadn't been burned. He called on Count Rostopchin and some acquaintances who had returned, and planned to leave for Petersburg in two days. Everyone was celebrating the victory; the ruined capital was buzzing with life and energy. Pierre was welcomed everywhere; everyone wanted to see him and hear about what he'd been through. He felt warmly disposed toward all the people he met, but was now instinctively on guard with everyone, careful not to tie himself down in any way. To every question put to him—whether important or trivial—such as: Where would he live? Would he rebuild? When was he going to Petersburg? Could he deliver a certain parcel?—he would answer: "Yes, perhaps," or "I think so," and so on.

He had heard that the Rostovs were in Kostroma, but thoughts of Natasha rarely came to him. When they did, it was only as a pleasant memory of the distant past. He felt free not only from social obligations but from the feeling that he had chosen to impose on himself.

On the third day after his arrival, he learned from the Drubetskoys that Princess Mary was in Moscow. The death, suffering, and final days of Prince Andrew had often occupied Pierre's thoughts and now came back to him with fresh vividness. Having heard over dinner that Princess Mary was in Moscow and living in her own house on Vozdvizhenka Street, which had survived the fire, he went to see her that same evening.
On his way to the house, Pierre kept thinking about Prince Andrew, about their friendship, their various meetings, and especially their last one at Borodino.

"Is it possible that he died in that bitter state of mind? Is it possible the meaning of life was never revealed to him before he died?" Pierre wondered. He thought of Karataev and his death, and involuntarily began comparing the two men—so different, yet somehow alike because of the love Pierre had felt for both and because both had lived and both had died.

Pierre drove up to the old prince's house in a very serious mood. The house had survived the fire; it showed signs of damage but its general appearance was unchanged. The old footman who greeted Pierre wore a stern expression, as if wanting to make the visitor feel that the absence of the old prince had not disrupted the household routine. He told Pierre that the princess had retired to her rooms and received visitors on Sundays.
"Please announce me. Perhaps she'll see me," said Pierre.
"Yes, sir," the man replied. "Please step into the portrait gallery."

A few minutes later the footman returned with Dessalles, who brought word from the princess that she would be very glad to see Pierre if he would excuse the informality and come upstairs to her rooms.

In a rather low room lit by a single candle sat the princess, and with her another person dressed in black. Pierre remembered that the princess always had lady companions, but who they were and what they were like he never knew. "This must be one of her companions," he thought, glancing at the woman in black.
The princess rose quickly to meet him and held out her hand.

"Yes," she said, looking at his changed face after he had kissed her hand, "so this is how we meet again. He spoke of you even at the very end," she went on, turning her eyes from Pierre to her companion with a shyness that surprised him.
"I was so glad to hear you were safe. It was the first good news we'd received in a long time."
Again the princess glanced at her companion with even more unease and was about to add something, but Pierre interrupted her.

"Imagine—I knew nothing about him!" he said. "I thought he'd been killed. Everything I know I heard secondhand from others. I only know that he ended up with the Rostovs... What a strange coincidence!"

Pierre spoke quickly and with animation. He glanced once at the companion's face, saw her attentive, kindly gaze fixed on him, and—as often happens when you're talking—felt somehow that this companion in the black dress was a good, kind, wonderful person who wouldn't interfere with his heartfelt conversation with Princess Mary.
But when he mentioned the Rostovs, Princess Mary's face showed still greater embarrassment. She again glanced rapidly from Pierre's face to that of the woman in the black dress and said:
"Don't you really recognize her?"

Pierre looked again at the companion's pale, delicate face with its dark eyes and distinctive mouth, and something near to him, long forgotten and more than sweet, looked back at him from those attentive eyes.

"But no, it can't be!" he thought. "This stern, thin, pale face that looks so much older! It can't be her. It just reminds me of her." But at that moment Princess Mary said, "Natasha!" And with difficulty, with effort, like a rusty door being forced open, a smile appeared on the face with the attentive eyes, and through that opening door came a fragrance from a long-forgotten world of happiness that Pierre had lost all thought of—especially now. It breathed over him, engulfed him, and swallowed him whole. When she smiled, there could be no doubt: it was Natasha, and he loved her.

In that moment, Pierre involuntarily revealed—to her, to Princess Mary, and above all to himself—a secret he hadn't even known he carried. He flushed with joy and painful emotion. He tried to hide his feelings. But the more he tried, the more clearly—more clearly than any words could have conveyed—he revealed to himself, to her, and to Princess Mary that he loved her.

"No, it's just the surprise," Pierre thought. But as soon as he tried to resume the conversation he'd been having with Princess Mary, he glanced again at Natasha, and a deeper flush spread across his face, and an even stronger wave of joy and agitation seized his heart.

Pierre had failed to notice Natasha because he hadn't expected to see her there, but he had failed to recognize her because the change in her since he'd last seen her was enormous. She had grown thin and pale. But it wasn't the thinness and pallor that made her unrecognizable—she was unrecognizable in the first moment because on that face, whose eyes had always shone with suppressed delight in life, there was now—when he first entered and glanced at her—not the slightest shadow of a smile. There were only eyes, watchful, kind, and sadly questioning.
Pierre's confusion was not mirrored by any confusion on Natasha's part—only by the pleasure that softly lit up her whole face.
